steps.text:
The chapel door was unlocked but stiff, and it swung on a hinge that needed a shoulder. Inside was one cool room, dust, a few leaning benches, and the smell of old incense sunk into the wood. Marta went straight to the back pew, set her lantern on it, and hauled the pew aside with a scrape that echoed off the low beams.

"Ring's there. Lift square, not with your back."

The flagstone came up between them on the second heave, heavier than its size promised, and beneath it a dark square opened with iron steps bolted into one wall, going down beyond what the light reached. Cold air breathed up out of it, dry and earthy, carrying a faint mineral smell like a deep well.

Marta hooked the flagstone's edge over an iron cramp set in the floor for exactly that purpose, then wedged the chapel door open with a flat stone from the pew corner. "Propped. There." She took up her lantern and went first down the steps, one hand on the wall, keys jingling at her hip. "Twenty-two steps. Count them coming up in the dark, if your lamp dies on you. Don't trust the dark to be short."

The stair turned once at a half-landing and went down again, the drizzle and grey daylight shrinking behind them until her lantern threw the only shadows. The walls changed partway—rough field stone giving over to dressed blocks, old and close-fitted, and names cut into them in a hand worn shallow by centuries.

At the bottom the steps ended in a round chamber no wider than the stair itself, and four arched mouths opened off it, one at each quarter—a central hall running north with side galleries branching left and right, all of it lost in dark beyond the lantern's reach. Bone-dry air, utterly still. Somewhere far off, water ticked once against stone and went quiet.

Marta held her lantern high and swept it slowly across the four mouths. Pillars stood in ranks down the main hall, pale in the light. She pointed with her chin at the nearest branching gallery.

"First level's all that—four galleries off this. Niches line the walls, and it's by the niches they stand up, so keep your back to the pillars, not the walls." She looked at him, lantern light catching the lines of her face. "I'll be up top, at the door. You call out or come up when you've done it—or before dark, whichever comes first. Don't make me come down after you."

The gallery mouth swallowed the lantern light within a few steps. Niches lined both walls, close-set as pigeonholes, some still sealed with carved slabs bearing names worn to shadows, others open and empty, a few holding the dry curled remains of those long unclaimed. Pillars stood down the middle of the passage at even intervals, their bases furred with a pale dust that took his footprints without sound.

Nothing moved. The air was so still his lamp flame stood upright like a painted thing, and his own footsteps came back to him doubled, as if someone walked an exact pace behind.

He kept to the pillars, lamp high, checking each niche before he passed it. The open ones were the ones to watch—Marta had said it true, and it played out: the sealed slabs were just stone, but where a niche gaped dark he gave it a longer look, staff ready in his other hand.

The third open niche was not empty.

The thing stood inside it where the light had shown emptiness a moment before—a dried shape wrapped in the rags of burial cloth, and it was not standing the way the dead stand when they're laid out. It had risen to the niche's mouth, and as the light touched it, its head came around with the slow creak of old leather, toward the lamp. Toward him.

It stepped out of the niche.

The cloth fell open from one arm as it moved, showing a brown forearm gone hard as wood, fingers long past the width of any living hand, flexing once. It came off the wall with a shuffling, deliberate step, its whole face a skull under a mask of drawn skin, and its hollow eye sockets found his light and held there—and it kept coming, one dragging step and then another, down from the niche into the gallery floor.
